entry.title: Dilemma Dynamics: replaying Nemotron’s cooperation decisions

link.title: Dilemma Dynamics: replaying Nemotron’s cooperation decisions

entry.content:
Exploring AI strategies, incentives and cooperation.

Updated 24 October 2026 with both completed temperature studies.

Open the interactive Dilemma Dynamics demo →

The demo opens Study replay: step through recorded Nemotron decisions, reveal both players’ actions together, and follow their points round by round. Switch to Results to explore aggregate findings, compare opponents, and download the report and public data. Everything in this demo uses saved results; viewing it requires no API key and incurs no inference charges.

I built Dilemma Dynamics to explore how language-model agents respond to incentives. Two completed temperature studies compare NVIDIA Nemotron Nano and Super in a repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma. Each round offers two actions: cooperate or defect. Mutual cooperation earns each player three points; unilateral defection earns five for the defector and zero for the cooperator; mutual defection earns one each. The objective is each player’s own cumulative points.

Does a draft help?

The study compares two procedures. Direct makes one thinking-off action request. Draft first makes a bounded thinking-on draft request, then a separate thinking-off action request conditioned on that draft. Both use the selected study temperature, 1 or 0, with top-p 1. Direct allows 128 output tokens; Draft allows 1,024 for the draft and 128 for the action. This comparison includes extra compute and an extra request; it does not isolate the effect of reasoning at equal cost.

Each temperature completed the same 24-block / 1,776-episode schedule: 1,536 episodes against four disclosed, committed opponent policies and 240 autonomous model dyads spanning all ten model/procedure pairings. That is 3,552 episodes in total, with matched IDs, episode order, stopping lengths, labels and seats. The studies ran on 22 October (temperature 1) and 23 October (temperature 0).

The benchmark measures the gap to the best achievable payoff against each disclosed opponent policy. Oracle loss records the expected own payoff forgone by a chosen action, assuming optimal play thereafter. Episode scores sum these gaps and normalise for the horizon; a smaller value means less achievable payoff left on the table. Cooperation is reported separately in autonomous play.

Model Temperature Direct mean loss Draft mean loss Draft − Direct Approx. 95% interval
Nemotron Nano 1 0.6889 0.4942 −0.1947 [−0.3077, −0.0983]
Nemotron Super 1 0.6150 0.3779 −0.2371 [−0.3095, −0.1735]
Nemotron Nano 0 0.7161 0.5616 −0.1545 [−0.2230, −0.0935]
Nemotron Super 0 0.4718 0.3763 −0.0956 [−0.1280, −0.0635]

Drafting lowered average benchmark loss for both models at both temperatures, but increased average loss against Tit-for-Tat. Lowering temperature improved Super Direct while Super Draft was nearly unchanged. Super’s drafting advantage therefore narrowed: the matched change in Draft-minus-Direct was +0.1415 (approximate 95% interval [+0.0840, +0.2066]). Nano’s change was +0.0402 [−0.0256, +0.1142], uncertain under this interval.

These intervals resample matched whole blocks within four presentation strata, with 20,000 bootstrap draws. Only six blocks per stratum are available; coverage and power are not established. This post-viewing sensitivity analysis has no multiplicity correction. Different execution dates, backend windows and recovery policies also differed, so changes cannot be attributed solely to temperature. Temperature zero does not guarantee deterministic hosted inference.

In autonomous play, mutual cooperation occurred in 189/2,060 rounds (9.2%) at temperature 1 and 244/2,060 (11.8%) at 0. Dependent rounds are not independent trials. These findings describe the tested schedules and procedures, rather than a general model ranking or a universal preferred temperature.

Try the recordings

  1. Open Study replay. The starting example is Nano Direct against Tit-for-Tat, with ten announced rounds in block 1 at temperature 0. Use the temperature selector to load the matched temperature-1 study. The starting condition was chosen by study metadata rather than its outcome.
  2. Reveal a round and inspect both choices and their payoffs. Compare the matched Direct and Draft procedures, or choose another condition, pairing, or block.
  3. Open Results to inspect both temperatures, matched changes, all ten autonomous pairings and recorded usage estimates.

The replay contains published actions, not reconstructed private drafts or beliefs. One recording illustrates play; it cannot estimate a procedure’s effect.

Scope and reproducibility

Both completed studies followed inspection of interrupted predecessor outcomes. The temperature-1 predecessor stopped after 339 episodes on HTTP 502. The first temperature-0 attempt stopped after 62 completed episodes on HTTP 529; a separately identified full recovery then completed the matched schedule. Interrupted and engineering observations are excluded. The findings remain descriptive, not a fresh confirmatory preregistration. Neither successful final run needed retries or recorded protocol failures.

Each completed final run used 17,124 successful requests. Usage-priced final inference estimates were $4.9278 at temperature 1 and $4.4791 at 0, excluding engineering and failed predecessors. These are estimates, not provider invoices or benchmark-only cost-effectiveness measurements. Viewing this site is free and sends no inference requests.

The public package supports reproduction of scores and estimates from revealed actions. It cannot independently authenticate provider identity, raw request history, or billing. The report explains the design, amendments, uncertainty, and limitations.

  • Read the report (PDF)
  • Read the methods and amendments
  • Download temperature-1 episode actions (JSON)
  • Download temperature-0 episode actions (JSON)
  • Download matched temperature changes (CSV)
  • Browse the public data and reproduction notes

Explore Dilemma Dynamics →

Extra: recreational board games

The full local app also offers Dots & Boxes and Tic-tac-toe as recreational extras for exploring tactics, search and visible-move play. These games sit outside the 3,552-episode cooperation evaluation. The public demo focuses on the dilemma study’s recordings and results; the repository setup guide explains how to run the full local app.

entry.title: Bayesian Orchestrator
entry.content:
Since March, I have been spending pretty much all my weekends doing… homework. Why? In March, I joined the AI Performance Engineering course at Nebius Academy, which also gave me the courage to try my own ideas and participate in the Nebius AI serverless challenge (and spend more weekends on that…). So here it goes!

There is a classic three-circle Venn diagram with cheap, fast, and good, where the intersection of these 3 bubbles is impossible. But how does one choose a possible combination depending on the task at hand, and whilst not being a trillionaire? Here, I address this problem in the context of LLM routing, and my motivation comes from a recent position paper on the need for Bayes in agentic AI orchestration.

It would be unreasonable to assume that an LLM can perform principled probabilistic reasoning (e.g. see this or this), and instead of trying to make LLMs more principled (which, in my very biased case, means more Bayesian), I built an external controller that tracks how reliable each model is and routes questions accordingly. The approach defines a hierarchical Bayesian reliability model to estimate the probability that each model will answer correctly, based on everything observed so far, that is the question type, subject matter, model identity, and picks the option with the best expected utility.

The utility function used here is rather simple but still balances accuracy against cost: utility = correctness − (cost scale × call cost), where one tunes the cost scale to express one’s preferences for increased costs versus accuracy.

Before you call a model, you can only use what you know ahead of time, which model it is, what subject the question is about, and how long the question is, which gives a pre-call probability estimate and determines which model to call first. After the model responds, the orchestrator gets more signals: how self-confident the model was, how long it took, and how many tokens it used. These go into a post-call probability estimate that determines whether the answer is given or the next model is called. If the first model’s answer looks doubtful, the orchestrator checks whether calling a second model is worth it. If the expected gain from a second call clears a threshold, it makes the call, then combines the answers using a Noisy-OR rule (which roughly says that if either model supports an answer, then that counts).

I test my idea on MMLU-Pro, a multiple-choice benchmark, with three models: two ~30B models and a 120B model, namely:

  • nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B

  • Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507

  • openai/gpt-oss-120b

For the setup, I ran it as a Nebius Serverless AI Job, which was a good fit because the workload is a finite batch evaluation: the container runs on CPU, model inference happens through APIs, every completed question-model call is checkpointed to persistent storage (meaning interrupted runs can continue without repeating paid calls).

The job samples 4000 MMLU-Pro questions, calls every configured model, checkpoints completed calls to persistent storage, fits Bayesian reliability models, and writes the final report, JSON summary, and plots. The repo is available on GitHub.

The results support the idea of Bayesian adaptive policy:

The adaptive policy called a second model on about one third of the questions. Compared to always using the big model, it’s more accurate but slightly more expensive; this could be tuned with the cost scale discussed above. The oracle looks cheap because it gets to retroactively pick the cheapest correct answer. In the real world, you don’t get to do that, so here I use the oracle as an upper bound.

LLMs themselves might be subtle predictors, but combined with Bayes-inspired reasoning, we can allocate resources more efficiently, manage costs and latencies, and adapt routing decisions as evidence accumulates. Workflows (Bayesian, please) over tools!

The project has gaps to fill, yet I feel good that I was able to build it up to its current state.

#NebiusServerlessChallenge

entry.summary: Or conductor for an orchestra of LLMs.
